chapter_title: RTL Viewer, Technology Map Viewer, and Design Visualization
chapter_summary:
One of the most powerful features of modern FPGA tools is the ability to visualize your design at multiple levels of abstraction. Quartus Prime provides three complementary viewers that show your design from the logical level down to the physical level. Learning to use these viewers effectively is essential for debugging, optimization, and understanding how HDL code maps to hardware.

**RTL Viewer:**
The RTL Viewer displays the generic netlist produced by the Analysis & Synthesis stage. It shows your design as a schematic of logic primitives: AND gates, OR gates, XOR gates, multiplexers, adders, comparators, and flip-flops. This is the closest representation to your mental model of the circuit. The RTL Viewer is invaluable for verifying that the synthesis tool correctly interpreted your HDL code.

For example, if you write a priority encoder in Verilog, the RTL Viewer should show a tree of multiplexers and comparators. If it shows something unexpected (like a latch or a counter), you know there is a bug in your code. Common issues caught in the RTL Viewer include:
- Inferred latches from incomplete if-else or case statements
- Unexpected counters from arithmetic operations inside always blocks
- Incorrect multiplexer structures from nested conditional operators
- Missing flip-flops from incorrect clock edge specifications

To use the RTL Viewer:
1. Compile the design through Analysis & Synthesis.
2. Go to **Tools > Netlist Viewers > RTL Viewer**.
3. Navigate through the hierarchy by double-clicking modules.
4. Zoom in to see individual gates and their connections.
5. Trace signals by clicking on wires and following the highlighted path.

**Technology Map Viewer:**
The Technology Map Viewer shows the netlist after technology mapping. It displays the actual FPGA primitives: Logic Elements (LEs), Adaptive Logic Modules (ALMs), DSP blocks, memory blocks, and I/O cells. This viewer is essential for understanding resource usage and identifying optimization opportunities.

For example, if you design a 16-tap FIR filter, the Technology Map Viewer will show how many DSP blocks and memory blocks are used. If the design uses too many LUTs, you might decide to use DSP blocks for the multipliers instead. If the design uses too many registers, you might pipeline the data path differently.

The Technology Map Viewer has two modes:
- **Post-Mapping:** Shows the netlist after technology mapping but before placement. This is useful for analyzing the logical structure of the mapped design.
- **Post-Fitting:** Shows the netlist after placement and routing. This is useful for analyzing the physical implementation, including the actual delay of each path.

To use the Technology Map Viewer:
1. Compile the design through the Fitter.
2. Go to **Tools > Netlist Viewers > Technology Map Viewer (Post-Mapping)** or **(Post-Fitting)**.
3. Navigate the hierarchy and zoom in to see individual LEs.
4. Click on an LE to see its LUT contents, flip-flop configuration, and carry chain connections.

**Chip Planner:**
The Chip Planner shows the physical layout of the design on the FPGA die. It displays the array of logic blocks, the routing channels, the I/O pads, and the hard blocks (DSP, memory, PLL). The Chip Planner is the most detailed view and is used for advanced optimization and debugging.

You can use the Chip Planner to:
- See where your design was placed on the FPGA die.
- Identify routing congestion (areas where too many signals compete for the same routing channels).
- Verify that critical paths are routed with short, low-delay connections.
- Manually place logic blocks for timing-critical designs.
- Locate unused resources for future expansion.

The Chip Planner uses color coding: logic elements are shown as small squares, routing wires as colored lines, and I/O pads as larger rectangles on the edges. You can search for specific nodes by name and see their physical location.

**Resource Utilization Report:**
After compilation, the Compilation Report window shows detailed resource usage. For a MAX 10 design, the report shows:
- Total logic elements used vs. available
- Total registers used vs. available
- Total memory bits used vs. available
- Total DSP blocks used vs. available
- Total PLLs used vs. available
- Pin usage (input, output, bidirectional)

The **Flow Summary** page gives a quick overview, while the **Fitter > Place Stage** page gives detailed per-region usage. If the design uses 90% of the logic elements, you have little room for expansion. If it uses only 10%, you might be able to use a smaller, cheaper FPGA.

screens.title: RTL Viewer, Technology Map Viewer, and Design Visualization
screens.subtitle: Understand how HDL becomes hardware, from logic netlists to physical placement

narration.text: In this lesson we explore three complementary visualization tools that reveal how your HDL maps to an FPGA. You will learn how the RTL Viewer shows a logical netlist that reflects what the synthesis stage inferred, how the Technology Map Viewer exposes the mapped primitives and resource usage after technology mapping and fitting, and how the Chip Planner reveals placement, routing, and congestion on the die. These views are not decorative: they are diagnostic. For example, the RTL Viewer can uncover an inferred latch caused by an incomplete conditional, the Technology Map Viewer can tell you whether multipliers became DSP blocks or LUT chains, and the Chip Planner can point to routing hotspots that cause timing violations. As you work through the chapter you will practice a short lab: compile a 4-bit ALU, trace the ADD path in the RTL Viewer, count logic elements in the Technology Map Viewer, and locate those elements in the Chip Planner. By the end of this chapter you will be able to ask focused questions like “Is this component synthesized into registers or combinational logic?” and take corrective action. Keep an eye out for common misconceptions, such as assuming synthesis preserves your code structure exactly — it often transforms it to meet mapping and timing constraints.

keyIdea.title: Visualize to verify and optimize
keyIdea.text: Use RTL for logical correctness, Technology Map for resource mapping, and Chip Planner for placement and routing decisions.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to verify the logical structure of your synthesized design, analyze how your HDL is mapped into FPGA primitives and resources, interpret detailed resource reports to guide optimizations, and inspect physical placement and routing to find timing or congestion issues. For example, after compiling a small ALU you will trace the ADD path in the RTL Viewer, confirm whether multipliers became DSP blocks in the Technology Map Viewer, and locate those mapped elements in the Chip Planner to check for routing congestion. You will also learn to read the resource utilization report to decide whether a design needs a larger device or whether pipelining or different primitives can reduce critical path length. These skills let you move from source-level guesses to evidence-based fixes, and they reduce the trial-and-error often seen when debugging timing or unexpected logic. Finally, you will complete a short lab that ties these objectives together and produces a short optimization report.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Lab and Assessment
screens.subtitle: Practice tasks and what to report

narration.text: This secondary objectives screen lays out the practical tasks you will perform and what to record. In the lab you will compile the 4-bit ALU from earlier chapters and perform three focused actions: trace the ADD operation in the RTL Viewer to confirm the logical netlist structure, open the Technology Map Viewer to count logic elements and inspect whether multipliers use DSP blocks, and then locate the mapped LEs in the Chip Planner to observe placement and routing. For each action you will write a short report: the logical structure you observed, the number of LEs and registers used, the physical region where the ALU elements were placed, and suggestions for optimization such as pipelining or using DSPs. This objective emphasizes evidence-based reporting so you can measure the effect of changes. The assessment idea included in this chapter asks you to identify an inferred latch from an RTL screenshot and describe the HDL fix. Practicing these tasks reinforces the full flow from code to physical hardware and helps you connect synthesis choices to timing outcomes.

screens.title: Why visualization matters
screens.subtitle: From mental model to evidence-based debugging

narration.text: Visualization bridges the gap between HDL text and physical hardware. When you write Verilog or VHDL you construct a mental model of how signals flow, but synthesis often restructures logic for mapping and timing. The RTL Viewer gives you a first evidence check: it shows the generic netlist of gates, multiplexers, adders and flip-flops synthesized from your code. That matters because a mismatch between your intent and the RTL is usually a coding bug, not a fitting issue. For example, an incomplete conditional can infer a latch; if you expect a register but see a latch in the RTL Viewer, you know to correct assignments in every branch. Visualization also helps optimization: seeing long chains of LUTs may prompt you to move multiplications into DSP blocks or add pipeline registers to shorten critical paths. A common misconception is to assume the fitter will hide inefficient logic — it will not magically eliminate functional misinterpretation or costly combinational chains. In practice, make visualization a routine part of compile-debug cycles: synthesize early, open the RTL Viewer, confirm key modules, then map and check resource use. This reduces surprise late in the flow and gives you concrete targets for fixes.

keyIdea.title: Visualization shortens debug cycles
keyIdea.text: Early use of viewers reveals synthesis mismatches and resource hotspots before fitting and placement.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Why visualization matters
Core Concept
Visualization connects code to hardware
Synthesis transforms HDL. Visualization reveals whether that transformation matches intent and where optimizations will help.
Definition
Visualization means inspecting RTL, mapped netlists, and physical placement to validate and optimize designs.
Concrete example
Finding an inferred latch in RTL from a missing else branch, then fixing HDL to ensure a register is synthesized instead.
Common mistake
Assuming the fitter will fix logic-level coding errors or hide inefficient combinational chains.
Key Takeaway

Always check the RTL netlist early to validate synthesis intent and prevent wasted effort later in the flow.

Quick diagnostic checklist
  • Compile through Analysis & Synthesis and open the RTL Viewer.
  • Confirm registers, multiplexers, and arithmetic units appear as expected.
  • If you see latches or unexpected counters, inspect your conditional branches and clocking statements.
  • Decide whether to refactor code, add default assignments, or add pipeline stages.
Analogy: think of RTL as the skeleton of your design. If the skeleton is wrong the rest of the body cannot be fixed by clothing or surface treatment. Fix the bones first.

narration.text: The RTL Viewer shows the generic netlist created by Analysis & Synthesis and is your first verification step after synthesis. Start by compiling the design to at least the Analysis & Synthesis stage. Then open Tools, Netlist Viewers, and choose RTL Viewer. In the viewer, navigate through the module hierarchy by double-clicking to open submodules, and zoom until individual gates and flip-flops are legible. A practical workflow is: compile, open RTL Viewer, inspect key modules, and trace signals from inputs to outputs. For example, when validating a priority encoder you expect a tree of comparators and multiplexers. If you instead see a latch, you should examine conditional statements in the HDL. Common mistakes include not setting default values for outputs in combinational blocks or mis-specifying clock edges so flip-flops are not generated. When tracing, click wires to highlight paths and follow highlighted nodes to see how signals propagate. Use this information to determine if a bug is in code or a synthesis interpretation, and then apply fixes such as adding default assignments or restructuring combinational logic. Finish by re-synthesizing to confirm the fix.

keyIdea.title: RTL Viewer workflow
keyIdea.text: Synthesize, open the RTL Viewer, trace signals, find inferred structures, and fix HDL before mapping.

Annotated RTL checklist

If you see unexpected state-holding elements, inspect always blocks and case statements to ensure full coverage of assignments.
After changes, re-run synthesis and confirm the RTL now matches expected hardware constructs.

screens.title: Technology Map Viewer: Post-Mapping vs Post-Fitting
screens.subtitle: Understand the difference and when to use each mode

narration.text: The Technology Map Viewer offers two important modes that provide different insights: Post-Mapping and Post-Fitting. Post-Mapping shows the netlist after technology mapping but before placement. It tells you how HDL constructs were translated into FPGA primitives such as logic elements, ALMs, DSP blocks, memory blocks, and input and output cells. Use Post-Mapping to evaluate resource choices: does an arithmetic block map into DSPs or into LUT chains? For example, a 16-tap FIR filter mapped into DSPs is preferable for performance, whereas LUT multipliers indicate potential for optimization. Post-Fitting shows the netlist after placement and routing. It adds physical detail: which LEs are placed next to each other, how carry chains are connected, and visible routing that affects path delays. Use Post-Fitting to analyze delay-critical paths and to locate congestion caused by clustering. A common misconception is that Post-Mapping equals final timing — only Post-Fitting shows actual placement-dependent delays. In practice, iterate: check Post-Mapping to reason about resource usage and Post-Fitting when timing or routing issues appear so you can make placement or pipelining decisions. Technology Map Viewer: Post-Mapping vs Post-Fitting means post-mapping = logical mapping to primitives; post-fitting = physical placement and routing with timing impact.. In practical terms, understand the difference and when to use each mode. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Two-map perspective
keyIdea.text: Post-Mapping = logical mapping to primitives; Post-Fitting = physical placement and routing with timing impact.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Technology Map Viewer
Comparison
Post-Mapping vs Post-Fitting
Choose the mode based on whether you need resource mapping or placement-dependent timing details.
Post-Mapping
Shows how logic maps to LEs, DSPs, memory blocks before placement. Use it to count resources and plan optimizations.
Post-Fitting
Shows placement, routing, and carry chain connections after fitting. Use it to inspect critical path delays and congestion.
Practical tip
Check Post-Mapping when exploring resource trade-offs; switch to Post-Fitting when timing or routing issues remain after mapping-level fixes.
Visual cues to look for
  • Clusters of LEs that suggest localized resource use or potential routing congestion.
  • DSP blocks used for arithmetic; if missing, consider changing synthesis directives or coding style.
  • Long LUT chains visible in Post-Mapping that may show up as long routed paths in Post-Fitting.
  • Carry chain alignment that affects addition speed and placement choices.
Key Takeaway

Use both views: mapping to select primitives, fitting to verify physical timing and routing constraints.

screens.title: Reading mapped primitives and LUT contents
screens.subtitle: What to inspect in the Technology Map Viewer

narration.text: The Technology Map Viewer reveals the actual primitives your design uses: logic elements (LEs), ALMs, DSP blocks, R A M blocks, and input and output cells. A careful read will show whether arithmetic units were implemented in dedicated DSPs or synthesized into LUTs and registers. Start by locating key modules and clicking individual LEs to inspect their LUT truth table, flip-flop configuration, and carry chain connections. For example, if a multiply became a LUT chain rather than a DSP, count how many LUTs it consumes and decide whether to rework the code or synthesis settings to target DSPs. Inspect flip-flop packing: many registers can share an LE; seeing few registers and many LUTs suggests a highly combinational design that may need pipelining. Another important element is carry chains: addition chains packed into carry structures are efficient; if you see broken carry chains, addition performance may suffer. A misconception is to treat resource numbers in isolation; instead cross-reference the LUT contents with the resource utilization report to decide whether to change coding style or constraints. Finally, use the Map Viewer to identify hotspots where manual resource or floorplanning might benefit timing-critical paths.

keyIdea.title: Inspect LUTs and carry chains
keyIdea.text: Determine whether arithmetic was placed into DSPs or LUTs and whether registers are packed efficiently.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Reading mapped primitives
Process Flow
Inspect LEs, LUT contents, and carry chains
Click mapped primitives to view LUT truth table, flip-flop config, and connections. This tells you how logic was implemented on silicon.
Check if arithmetic units used DSPs. If not, quantify LUT cost and consider guidance to use DSPs for multipliers.
Inspect register packing: many registers in few LEs indicates efficient packing. Low register count with high LUTs suggests heavy combinational logic.
Look for contiguous carry chains for efficient adders. Broken chains may indicate suboptimal placement or synthesis choices.
Note LUT contents to detect synthesized state machines or large truth tables that might be simplified or implemented differently.
Quick example
A multiply that consumes several LUTs likely should be redirected to a DSP block. Use synthesis attributes or coding patterns that infer DSPs, then re-check the Map Viewer.
Key Takeaway

Reading primitive internals guides decisions to change coding style, add constraints, or apply floorplanning to improve performance.

screens.title: Chip Planner basics
screens.subtitle: From bird's-eye view to region zoom and node search

narration.text: The Chip Planner shows your design mapped onto the physical FPGA die. It displays arrays of logic blocks, routing channels, input and output pads, and hard blocks such as DSPs, memory, and PLLs. Use it to find where the fitter placed your LEs and how routing connects them. Start with a bird's-eye view to identify clusters, then zoom into regions to inspect individual logic squares and routed wires. You can search for specific nodes by name to highlight their exact physical location. The Chip Planner is essential for diagnosing routing congestion: crowded routing channels or widely separated related elements often cause timing failures. For timing-critical paths, manual placement of logic or floorplanning can reduce interconnect delay. Be mindful that Chip Planner uses color coding: small squares for logic elements, colored lines for routing, and larger edge rectangles for input and output. One misconception is that placement is purely automatic; manual intervention or constraints may be necessary for high-performance designs. After identifying a congested region, try pipelining, changing placement constraints, or redistributing logic to reduce routing competition and improve timing. Chip Planner basics means use chip planner to find placement clusters, routing congestion, and to plan manual placement or floorplanning for timing fixes.. In practical terms, from bird's-eye view to region zoom and node search. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Physical inspection
keyIdea.text: Use Chip Planner to find placement clusters, routing congestion, and to plan manual placement or floorplanning for timing fixes.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Chip Planner basics
Process Flow
Inspect placement, routing, and congestion
Use bird's-eye view for global patterns, zoom for per-LE details, and search to locate named nodes for precise inspection.
Bird's-eye: locate dense clusters and large unused regions for potential floorplanning or expansion.
Zoom in: inspect routing lines and how carries or critical paths are physically connected; note long wires or detours.
Search nodes: find the physical location of a logic element by name to correlate with mapped resources and the report.
Key Takeaway

Chip Planner turns resource counts into spatial decisions: placement matters for timing and congestion and should guide optimization choices.

Visual legend
Logic element
Routing wire

Example action: when a critical net crosses a congested channel, consider adding a pipeline stage or moving related logic closer together to shorten the routed path and reduce delay.

screens.title: Resource Utilization Report
screens.subtitle: How to read usage numbers and regional summaries

narration.text: The Compilation Report gives concrete metrics that guide device selection and optimization. It lists totals and per-resource usage: total logic elements used versus available, registers used, memory bits used, DSP blocks used, PLLs, and pin usage. Start with the Flow Summary for a quick health check: are you using 90 percent of logic elements or only 10 percent? High usage means limited room for features or rework; low usage may suggest a smaller device could be chosen. Then inspect the Fitter › Place Stage page for per-region utilization; this reveals imbalance where one area of the die is nearly full while others are sparse, which often causes routing congestion. For example, if your ALU uses many LEs and most are clustered in a single region, the fitter may struggle to route critical nets. A common misconception is to treat a single resource count as sufficient; instead correlate logic element counts with registers, memory, and DSP usage. If you have many LUTs but few registers, the design may be overly combinational and need pipelining. Use these numbers to select optimizations: pipelining, floorplanning, or switching arithmetic to DSP blocks when available.

keyIdea.title: Numbers drive decisions
keyIdea.text: Use totals and per-region reports to pick optimization strategies such as pipelining, floorplanning, or device changes.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Resource Utilization Report
Definition
Read totals and region summaries
Start with Flow Summary then inspect Fitter → Place Stage for per-region usage and imbalances that cause routing issues.
Total logic elements used vs available
Total registers used vs available
Total memory bits and DSP blocks used
Pin usage and per-region occupancy
Key Takeaway

Resource numbers identify when to change device size, add pipelining, or target DSPs for arithmetic-heavy designs.

Practical interpretations
If LEs are near capacity, plan for a larger device or prioritise reduction of logic through refactoring.
If DSPs are scarce but multipliers are implemented with LUTs, refactor code or use synthesis directives to prefer DSP inference.
Per-region imbalance often causes routing congestion; consider floorplanning or redistributing logic.

screens.title: Common RTL issues visible in the RTL Viewer
screens.subtitle: Inferred latches, unexpected counters, and missing flip-flops

narration.text: Several common RTL-level issues are best caught in the RTL Viewer. Inferred latches occur when combinational signals are not assigned in every branch of an if-else or case statement; the synthesizer preserves previous values by creating storage. If you expect purely combinational behavior but find a latch, add default assignments or refactor the conditional so all outputs are assigned in every branch. Unexpected counters can appear when arithmetic operations occur in clocked or combinational always blocks without clear reset or control; the RTL Viewer will show chains of flip-flops creating counting behavior. Missing flip-flops are often the result of incorrect clock edge specification or using combinational constructs where registers were intended. Another scenario is incorrect multiplexer structures created by nested conditional operators; the RTL Viewer helps you verify that multiplexer trees match your algorithm. For each of these issues, the fix is a code change: complete assignments, correct clocking constructs, or change expressions to clearer state-machine style. The viewer gives you direct evidence so you fix the HDL rather than guessing at fitter interventions. Common RTL issues visible in the RTL Viewer means use rtl evidence to correct hdl for latches, counters, and clocking issues before moving to mapping or placement.. In practical terms, inferred latches, unexpected counters, and missing flip-flops. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Fix code, not fitter
keyIdea.text: Use RTL evidence to correct HDL for latches, counters, and clocking issues before moving to mapping or placement.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Common RTL issues
Core Concept
Detect and fix RTL problems
Use the RTL Viewer to find inferred latches, counters, and incorrect registers and correct the HDL accordingly.
Inferred latch: add default assignment in combinational blocks or complete case branches.
Unexpected counter: check arithmetic inside always blocks and ensure intended register behavior.
Missing flip-flop: verify clock edge and synchronous assignments to produce registers.
Example scenario
Given a combinational mux whose output retains previous value, the RTL Viewer shows a latch. The fix is to assign the output in every conditional branch or provide a default at the start of the combinational block.
Pro tip: add explicit default assignments to avoid accidental latches.
Check your clocking: inconsistent edges silently change registers into combinational elements.

screens.title: Optimization strategies guided by viewers
screens.subtitle: When to pipeline, when to use DSPs, and when to floorplan

narration.text: Viewers help you choose targeted optimization strategies. If the Technology Map Viewer shows heavy LUT use for multipliers, consider rewriting code or adding synthesis attributes to infer DSP blocks for multiplications. If the resource utilization report shows many LUTs but few registers, add pipeline stages to break long combinational paths and improve timing; verify the effect by re-running synthesis and checking the Map Viewer for reduced LUT chains. When the Chip Planner reveals a region near capacity or severe routing congestion, consider floorplanning or manual placement of performance-critical logic to spread resource use and shorten routes. Use small, incremental changes: add a pipeline register, re-synthesize, and check whether critical path delays improved in Post-Fitting. A common trap is making broad changes without measurement; viewers provide immediate feedback so you can measure the effect of each change. For example, after adding a pipeline stage to an ALU, verify in the RTL Viewer that registers were added, in the Map Viewer that LEs reflect the change, and in the Chip Planner that routed paths are shortened. This evidence-based loop reduces guesswork and converges on a reliable optimization.

keyIdea.title: Measure, change, re-measure
keyIdea.text: Use viewers to pick small, measurable optimizations: pipeline, target DSPs, or floorplan based on evidence.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Optimization strategies
Process Flow
Optimize using viewer evidence
Pick a single hypothesis, apply a small change, and re-measure through viewers and the report.
Pipeline long combinational paths when Map Viewer shows long LUT chains or report shows low register usage relative to LUTs.
Switch multipliers to DSPs if Map Viewer shows LUT-based multiplication and DSPs are available.
Floorplan or manually place critical logic if the Chip Planner shows per-region saturation or routing congestion.
Example iteration
Add a pipeline register to shorten a critical path, re-synthesize, confirm registers in RTL Viewer, check reduced LUT chains in Map Viewer, and verify shorter routed wires in Chip Planner.
Avoid large-scale rewrites without intermediate checks. Each small change should be validated by the viewers so you know it had the intended effect.

screens.title: Lab walkthrough: 4-bit ALU tasks
screens.subtitle: Trace ADD in RTL, count LEs, and locate in Chip Planner

narration.text: This lab ties the viewers together using the 4-bit ALU from Chapter 4.2. First, compile the ALU through Analysis & Synthesis and open the RTL Viewer. Trace the signal path for the ADD operation from inputs through the adder and output. Confirm you see adders and expected multiplexers; if not, inspect HDL branches and registers. Second, run the fitter and open the Technology Map Viewer in Post-Mapping mode. Count the number of LEs and registers used by the ALU and note whether multipliers or arithmetic structures used DSP blocks or LUT chains. Third, switch the Map Viewer to Post-Fitting or open the Chip Planner to locate those mapped LEs on the die. Use the node search feature to find the ALU instance by name and observe clustering or routing lines that could create congestion. Record: (1) the logical structure from RTL Viewer, (2) LEs and registers counts, (3) physical locations in the Chip Planner, and (4) suggestions for optimization such as pipelining or DSP usage. This evidence will form the basis of your short report and demonstrate practical mastery of the visualization workflow.

keyIdea.title: Lab evidence loop
keyIdea.text: Trace, measure, and locate: produce a short report linking RTL structure, resource counts, and physical locations to optimization choices.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Lab walkthrough
ALU lab steps
Follow these steps and capture screenshots or notes for your report.
Step 1 — RTL Viewer

narration.text: Assessments in this chapter probe your ability to read viewers and propose fixes. Two representative scenarios are useful practice. Scenario A: an RTL Viewer screenshot shows a latch on an output that should be combinational. The key diagnosis is an incomplete if-else or case assignment. The HDL fix is to add default assignments at the start of the combinational process or ensure each branch assigns the output. Scenario B: the Technology Map Viewer reports 100 LEs used and only 20 registers. This suggests the design is mostly combinational. Interpretations include potential long combinational paths, timing risks, and the need to add pipelining or restructure logic. For each scenario, the assessment asks you to explain the cause, the evidence in the viewer, and the precise HDL or design-level correction you would make. When answering, include the viewer evidence, a short HDL change, and how you would re-check the fix in synthesis and the map or chip views. These practices train you to justify fixes with visual evidence rather than guesswork. Scoring: identify the viewer evidence, propose a specific fix, and describe how you would verify the fix across RTL Viewer, Technology Map Viewer, and Chip Planner.

narration.text: Keep these core ideas in mind as you work through visualizations. The RTL Viewer is for logical verification: it reveals whether synthesis interpreted your HDL correctly and surfaces issues like inferred latches or missing registers. The Technology Map Viewer shows how logic maps to FPGA primitives and is the primary tool for resource analysis, revealing whether arithmetic uses DSPs or LUT chains and how registers are packed. The Chip Planner is your physical inspection tool: it shows placement, routing and congestion on the die and guides manual placement or floorplanning when timing or routing problems remain. Finally, the resource utilization report quantifies LEs, registers, memory, DSPs and pins so you can make device selection and optimization decisions. Use viewers together in an evidence-driven loop: synthesize, inspect RTL, map resources, check placement, apply a small fix, and re-measure. This cycle turns guessing into measured improvements.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Compact concept cards for quick recall

narration.text: As a quick recap: use the RTL Viewer to confirm synthesis intent and find coding bugs like inferred latches; use the Technology Map Viewer to count and inspect mapped primitives and decide whether arithmetic should use DSPs; use the Chip Planner to diagnose routing congestion and to plan manual placement for timing-critical logic; and use the Compilation Report to judge device sizing and to spot per-region imbalances. When optimizing, follow a tight loop: hypothesize, change code or constraints, recompile, and verify the result across viewers. This approach turns visualization into an active debugging and optimization practice rather than a passive display. Keep this loop in your toolkit and apply it to the ALU lab and future designs to reduce surprises and improve timing predictably.
